questions.stem: Leadership is important in change management mainly because effective leaders:
options: can impose change without needing to review its results afterwards
set a clear vision and inspire employees to commit to the change
remove any need to communicate with employees about the change
can make sure that change happens without any resistance at all
questions.explanation: Leaders give a direction for change and build the trust and commitment employees need to accept it. Even strong leadership cannot remove all resistance, and the results of change still need to be reviewed.

questions.stem: The chief executive of a Geelong manufacturer visits every site to explain why change is needed, listens to staff concerns and models the new ways of working herself. This shows:
options: a laissez-faire style that leaves staff to manage the change
effective leadership that builds trust and support for change
a high-risk strategy of manipulation to overcome resistance
organisational inertia slowing down the change process
questions.explanation: By communicating openly, listening and leading by example, the chief executive builds the trust that helps staff accept change. Manipulation involves misleading or selective information, which is not described.

questions.stem: A café's key performance indicators show a rise in customer complaints about slow service and wrong orders. Which management strategy most directly responds to this?
options: global outsourcing of the café's bookkeeping to another country
overseas manufacture of the café's takeaway cups and lids
cost cutting by reducing the number of staff on each shift
staff training in order-taking and service procedures
questions.explanation: The complaints point to service errors, which training in procedures directly addresses. Cutting staff numbers would probably slow service further and increase complaints.

questions.stem: A Gold Coast hotel's key performance indicators show high staff absenteeism and staff turnover. Which management strategy most directly addresses these results?
options: initiating Just in Time ordering of food for the hotel's kitchen
staff motivation strategies such as support and career advancement
global sourcing of linen and toiletries from cheaper overseas suppliers
increased investment in robotics to clean the hotel's rooms
questions.explanation: High absenteeism and turnover suggest low motivation and job satisfaction, so motivation strategies target the cause. Global sourcing and Just in Time affect inputs and costs, not how staff feel about their work.

questions.stem: A Wodonga packaging plant's wastage KPI has risen for three years, and it often holds large stocks of finished goods that later have to be thrown away. Which strategy best responds to this?
options: initiating lean production techniques such as pull and zero defects
changing to a laissez-faire management style for production staff
moving the plant's production overseas to a lower-cost country
increasing the advertising budget to sell the stockpiled goods
questions.explanation: Lean techniques such as pull produce only what customers order, cutting excess stock, while zero defects reduces faulty output, so both lower wastage. Moving production overseas would shift the problem rather than fix the wasteful processes.

questions.stem: A mining company closes one mine and moves its workers and heavy equipment to a new site it is opening. This management strategy is:
options: redeployment of resources
global outsourcing
cost cutting
innovation
questions.explanation: Redeployment means moving natural, labour or capital resources to where they can be used more effectively, as with moving staff and equipment to the new mine. Global outsourcing would involve contracting another business overseas to do the work.

questions.stem: As a management strategy, innovation involves:
options: introducing new or improved products, processes or ideas
cutting costs by reducing the number of employees in the business
buying the business's inputs from suppliers in other countries
moving labour and equipment between different parts of the business
questions.explanation: Innovation is creating and introducing something new or improved, whether a product, process or way of doing business. Moving labour and equipment within the business is redeployment of resources.

questions.stem: A business facing falling net profit cuts its training budget and reduces staff numbers. Which is the most likely long-term risk of this strategy?
options: lower morale and service quality, which may lead to more complaints and fewer sales
a guaranteed rise in market share because the business can now cut its prices
a rise in labour costs, because fewer employees are left on the payroll
an immediate increase in the skills of the staff who remain in the business
questions.explanation: Cost cutting can lift profit in the short term, but fewer and less-trained staff may reduce quality and morale, which can hurt sales later. Lower costs do not guarantee higher market share.

questions.stem: A Brisbane toy company's market share is falling because rivals keep launching new products. Which management strategy most directly addresses this?
options: global outsourcing of the company's payroll processing
redeployment of office furniture to a new head office
innovation to develop new products that customers want
sanction strategies for sales staff who miss their targets
questions.explanation: The business is losing sales to rivals' new products, so innovation that develops new products tackles the cause. Sanctions on sales staff do not change what the business has to sell.

questions.stem: A survey shows that staff at a Shepparton distribution centre feel ignored and morale is low under a manager who makes every decision alone. Which strategy best responds to this?
options: adopting Porter's lower cost strategy across the whole business
global sourcing of packing materials from overseas suppliers
increasing the number of quality control inspections each day
changing to a consultative or participative management style
questions.explanation: Staff feel left out of decisions, so a style that seeks or shares their input addresses the cause of low morale. Sourcing and inspection strategies deal with inputs and quality, not with how staff are managed.

questions.stem: A Launceston accounting firm finds that its rate of productivity growth lags behind its rivals' because staff enter data by hand. Which strategy most directly responds?
options: overseas manufacture of the firm's printed client reports
increased investment in technology that automates data entry
a change to an autocratic management style for all decisions
cutting the training budget to reduce the firm's expenses
questions.explanation: Automating manual data entry lets staff produce more in the same time, directly lifting productivity. Cutting training would be more likely to reduce productivity than raise it.

questions.stem: Which is a strategy for developing a positive corporate culture?
options: keeping the business's values statement hidden from staff
rewarding behaviour that conflicts with the stated values
recruiting staff whose values clash with the business's
managers modelling the desired values in their own behaviour
questions.explanation: When managers act on the values they promote, employees see what is expected and are more likely to adopt it. Rewarding behaviour that conflicts with stated values widens the gap between official and real culture.

questions.stem: To build a culture of safety, a Pilbara mining contractor starts every shift with a safety briefing, rewards teams with no incidents and promotes supervisors who champion safety. Which strategies for developing culture is it using?
options: global outsourcing and redeployment
quality control and quality assurance
rituals and rewarding the desired behaviour
manipulation and threat
questions.explanation: Regular shift briefings are a ritual, and rewards and promotions reinforce the safe behaviour the business wants, so they shape the real culture. Manipulation and threat are high-risk strategies for overcoming resistance, not for building culture.

questions.stem: Orbit Software's managers publicly promote innovation, but staff who suggest new ideas are told to 'stick to the plan'. Which strategy would best align the real culture with the official culture?
options: rewriting the mission statement to stress innovation even more strongly
introducing sanctions for staff who suggest ideas outside the plan
outsourcing the company's product design work to an overseas firm
managers modelling and rewarding the sharing of new ideas
questions.explanation: The real culture discourages ideas, so managers must change their own behaviour and reward idea sharing for the culture to match the stated value. Rewriting the mission statement changes only the official culture, which is already pro-innovation.

questions.stem: Which is one of the five disciplines of Senge's Learning Organisation?
options: shared vision
the drive to bond
unfreezing
organisational inertia
questions.explanation: Senge's five disciplines are personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning and systems thinking. Unfreezing is the first step of Lewin's Three-step Change Model.

questions.stem: In Senge's Learning Organisation, systems thinking means:
options: seeing the business as a whole made up of interrelated parts
each person committing to their own lifelong learning and growth
teams learning together through open and honest dialogue
challenging the deeply held assumptions that shape how people act
questions.explanation: Systems thinking, the fifth discipline, is understanding how the parts of a business affect each other and the whole, and it ties the other four disciplines together. Lifelong personal learning is personal mastery, and challenging assumptions is mental models.

questions.stem: A Darwin engineering firm funds each employee's chosen professional development and encourages every staff member to keep learning throughout their career. Which of Senge's disciplines does this reflect?
options: systems thinking
shared vision
mental models
personal mastery
questions.explanation: Personal mastery is each individual's commitment to continual learning and developing their own capabilities. Shared vision concerns a common picture of the future that the whole business works towards.

questions.stem: Managers at a family-owned printer hold workshops to question the long-held belief that 'our customers will always want printed catalogues'. Which of Senge's disciplines does this reflect?
options: team learning
systems thinking
mental models
personal mastery
questions.explanation: Mental models are the deeply held assumptions that shape how people see the business, and a learning organisation brings them into the open and challenges them. Team learning is about groups learning together through dialogue, rather than testing a particular belief.

questions.stem: Project teams at a Melbourne engineering consultancy meet after every project to discuss openly what went well and what they learnt from their mistakes. Which of Senge's disciplines does this reflect?
options: shared vision
team learning
mental models
personal mastery
questions.explanation: Team learning occurs when groups think and learn together through open dialogue, so the team's knowledge grows beyond what individuals know. Personal mastery is about each individual's own development.

questions.stem: Staff at every level of a Hobart tourism business help shape a picture of where the business should be in five years, and they feel genuinely committed to it. Which of Senge's disciplines does this reflect?
options: shared vision
systems thinking
team learning
mental models
questions.explanation: A shared vision is a common picture of the future that staff help build and so genuinely commit to, rather than one imposed by management. Systems thinking is about seeing how all the parts of the business connect.

questions.stem: Why is a learning organisation usually better placed to implement change successfully?
options: employees are trained to follow every instruction without question
it has no need to review KPIs after the change has been made
change in it is driven only by senior managers acting alone
staff keep learning and adapting, so they are more open to new ideas
questions.explanation: In a learning organisation, continual learning and a positive culture for change mean staff expect and welcome new ways of working, which lowers resistance. Following instructions without question is the opposite of Senge's emphasis on dialogue and learning.

questions.stem: Which is a low-risk strategy for overcoming employee resistance to change?
options: threat
organisational inertia
empowerment
manipulation
questions.explanation: Empowerment gives employees a role in decisions about the change, which builds ownership and lowers resistance with little risk. Manipulation and threat are high-risk strategies, and organisational inertia is a restraining force, not a strategy.

questions.stem: Before introducing new software, managers hold briefings to explain why it is needed and how it will affect each role. Which low-risk strategy are they using?
options: empowerment
support
communication
incentives
questions.explanation: Communication means informing employees of the reasons for change and its effects, which reduces fear of the unknown. Empowerment would involve giving staff a say in decisions about the change.

questions.stem: A supermarket chain lets each store's staff decide how to reorganise their own rosters to fit new opening hours. Which low-risk strategy is this?
options: manipulation
empowerment
communication
incentives
questions.explanation: Giving staff the authority to make decisions about how the change is carried out is empowerment, which builds ownership of the change. Communication only informs staff, without giving them decision-making power.

questions.stem: A business offers training sessions and confidential counselling to staff who are anxious about new technology. Which low-risk strategy is this?
options: threat
communication
support
incentives
questions.explanation: Support helps employees cope with change through training, counselling and resources. Incentives would offer a reward for accepting the change.

questions.stem: A bank pays a bonus to every employee who completes training in its new customer system by a set date. Which strategy is this?
options: incentives
support
manipulation
empowerment
questions.explanation: Incentives offer rewards, such as bonuses, to encourage employees to accept change. Support would focus on helping staff cope rather than rewarding them.

questions.stem: To win support for a restructure, managers show staff only the favourable parts of a consultant's report and hide its finding that 40 jobs would be cut. Which strategy is this?
options: empowerment
manipulation
threat
communication
questions.explanation: Manipulation means influencing employees by giving them selective, misleading or false information. Threat would involve warning staff of negative consequences if they do not accept the change.

questions.stem: A manager tells staff that anyone who has not started using the new system by Friday will lose their weekend shifts. Which strategy is this?
options: manipulation
incentives
support
threat
questions.explanation: Threat uses the warning of negative consequences, here the loss of shifts, to force acceptance of change. Incentives would reward staff for using the new system rather than punish them for not using it.

questions.stem: Why are manipulation and threat described as high-risk strategies for overcoming resistance?
options: they take much longer to work than low-risk strategies
they cost far more to put in place than incentives do
staff who resent or uncover them may lose trust, which can increase resistance
they are always illegal under Australian workplace laws
questions.explanation: These strategies may get quick compliance, but if employees discover the deception or resent the pressure, trust and morale suffer and resistance can grow. They are usually fast and cheap rather than slow or costly.

questions.stem: In which situation might a manager consider using a high-risk strategy such as threat?
options: when there is plenty of time to consult staff about the change
when employees already strongly support the proposed change
when the main aim is to build long-term trust with employees
when change is urgent and low-risk strategies have already failed
questions.explanation: High-risk strategies may be used as a last resort when change must happen quickly and other strategies have not worked. If staff already support the change or there is time to consult, low-risk strategies are more appropriate.

questions.stem: Which shows the steps of Lewin's Three-step Change Model in order?
options: change, unfreeze, refreeze
refreeze, change, unfreeze
unfreeze, refreeze, change
unfreeze, change, refreeze
questions.explanation: Lewin's model first unfreezes the current situation, then moves to the new way of operating, and finally refreezes it as the new norm. Change cannot come first, because the old ways must be unfrozen before people accept something new.

questions.stem: Managers at a Ballarat call centre present data on falling customer satisfaction and explain why the current way of working cannot continue. Which step of Lewin's Three-step Change Model is this?
options: evaluating the response
unfreeze
change
refreeze
questions.explanation: Unfreezing prepares people for change by showing why the status quo cannot continue and creating a sense of need. The change step is when the new methods are actually introduced.

questions.stem: Staff at a Geelong warehouse are trained in a new picking process and begin using it, with managers on the floor to help. Which step of Lewin's Three-step Change Model is this?
options: weighting
change
unfreeze
refreeze
questions.explanation: The change, or moving, step is when the new process is introduced and staff begin to use it, with training and support. Refreezing comes later, when the new process is locked in as normal practice.

questions.stem: After a new system has been introduced, managers update company policies, reward staff who use it and include it in performance reviews. Which step of Lewin's Three-step Change Model is this?
options: unfreeze
ranking
refreeze
change
questions.explanation: Refreezing embeds the change as the new norm through policies, rewards and procedures so staff do not slip back. The change step is the earlier stage when the system was first put in place.

questions.stem: If a business skips the refreeze step of Lewin's Three-step Change Model, the most likely outcome is that:
options: employees drift back to their old ways of working over time
the change will never begin, because no one is prepared for it
employee resistance to the change will fall to zero
the driving forces for change will become restraining forces
questions.explanation: Without refreezing, the new behaviours are not reinforced, so people tend to return to familiar habits. The change has already begun, so a lack of preparation is a problem of skipping unfreezing, not refreezing.

questions.stem: Lewin's two models are often used together. During the unfreeze step, managers would most usefully:
options: weaken restraining forces, for example by explaining the reasons for change
strengthen restraining forces so that the business remains stable
reward the new behaviour so that it becomes the accepted norm
train staff in how to carry out the new process from day to day
questions.explanation: Unfreezing prepares the business for change, so reducing resistance, for example through communication, helps the driving forces outweigh the restraining forces. Rewarding the new behaviour belongs to refreezing, and training in the new process belongs to the change step.

questions.stem: A supermarket chain introduces self-service checkouts in all its stores. Which is a likely effect of this change on its employees?
options: new contracts to supply and service checkout machines
fewer checkout hours and a need to retrain for other roles
higher dividends as a result of lower labour costs
shorter queues and less time spent waiting to pay
questions.explanation: Self-service checkouts replace some cashier work, so employees may lose hours and need retraining. Higher dividends affect owners, shorter queues affect customers, and new contracts affect suppliers.

questions.stem: A Victorian food manufacturer switches to global sourcing of its inputs. Which stakeholder group is most likely to be negatively affected?
options: its customers, who will no longer be able to buy its products
its local Australian suppliers, which may lose contracts
its overseas suppliers, which will lose the business's orders
its owners, who will pay much higher prices for inputs
questions.explanation: Buying inputs from overseas means the business's existing local suppliers may lose orders and revenue. The overseas suppliers gain business, and global sourcing is usually chosen to lower, not raise, input costs.

questions.stem: A regional town's largest employer moves its production overseas. Which is the most likely effect on the general community?
options: higher wages for workers who remain in the local area
job losses that reduce spending at other local businesses
more local jobs as the business expands its local factory
new contracts for local suppliers to provide its inputs
questions.explanation: When a major employer moves production away, local jobs are lost and households spend less, which hurts other businesses in the town. The business is closing local production, not expanding it or buying more locally.

questions.stem: For managers, a major change in a business often means:
options: a guaranteed increase in dividends from their shares
lower prices and better quality for their purchases
new orders for the inputs that they supply
extra workload and the need to develop new skills
questions.explanation: Managers must plan, lead and implement change, which adds to their workload and may require new skills, and their own roles may change. Dividends are an owner interest, and new orders affect suppliers.

questions.stem: Which is a corporate social responsibility consideration when implementing change?
options: choosing the cheapest overseas supplier without checking its conditions
supporting redundant employees with retraining and outplacement
maximising short-term profit regardless of the effect on others
keeping all plans for the change secret from the business's staff
questions.explanation: Socially responsible change considers its effects on stakeholders, such as helping employees who lose their jobs find new work. Choosing a supplier without checking its working conditions ignores the business's ethical obligations.

questions.stem: A clothing brand plans to switch to a new overseas manufacturer to cut costs. Which action best reflects corporate social responsibility in this change?
options: auditing the manufacturer's working conditions and environmental practices
choosing the manufacturer only on the basis of the lowest quoted price
announcing the switch without telling the existing suppliers in advance
keeping the location of the new manufacturer secret from its customers
questions.explanation: CSR means the business considers the welfare of workers and the environment, not just cost, so checking the manufacturer's practices is responsible. Choosing on price alone ignores these obligations.

questions.stem: Why should managers review key performance indicators after implementing a change?
options: to remove the need for the business to make any future changes
to measure whether the change has achieved its intended outcomes
to find out which employees resisted so that they can be dismissed
because the law requires every business to publish its KPIs each month
questions.explanation: Comparing KPIs after the change with earlier results or targets shows whether the transformation worked and whether further action is needed. Reviewing KPIs is about evaluating the change, not punishing staff.

questions.stem: Before a staff training program, a Bendigo café received 120 complaints a month; six months after it, complaints were 80 a month. Staff absenteeism stayed at 4 per cent. Which is the best evaluation?
options: the program seems to have improved service but has not reduced absenteeism
the program has failed overall, because staff absenteeism did not fall
the program has cut complaints by 50 per cent and also reduced absenteeism
the program has caused the rate of staff absenteeism to rise
questions.explanation: Complaints fell by 40, which is 40 ÷ 120 = about 33 per cent, suggesting better service, while absenteeism was unchanged. Calling the fall 50 per cent divides by the new figure of 80 instead of the original 120.
